clue.text: Current battle in France

definitions.meaning: a current is a flowing river, here a French one
the First World War Battle of the ... was fought on that river east of Paris

explanation.surface: A news item about a battle now being fought in France.
explanation.definitionFit: The Marne is a French river (a current of water) and gave its name to two First World War battles.

clue.text: Sounds as if what the usherette did was in error

indicators.note: says the following spoken phrase is heard like the entered word

parts.note: a cinema usherette, a young woman or miss, guided people to their seats

explanation.surface: An usherette went wrong in what she did.
explanation.walkthrough: An usherette was the woman with a torch who showed British cinemagoers to their seats.
explanation.definitionFit: Misguided means mistaken, acting on wrong judgement.

clue.text: Assessment a pound — it's beastly !

definitions.note: the definition is a phrase meaning it is an animal, the answer being the animal itself

parts.note: a rate is an assessment of value or of local tax
L is the abbreviation for pound, from Latin libra

explanation.surface: A complaint that an assessment of a pound is horrible.
explanation.definitionFit: The ratel is the honey badger, a fierce African animal.

clue.text: Scholarly head of a lady of '25?

definitions.text: Scholarly head of a lady of '25?

parts.words: Scholarly head of a lady of '25?
parts.note: a hairstyle named after a famous school, a short boyish cut fashionable among women in 1925

explanation.definitionFit: A very short sleek haircut for women, named after the school, was the rage in the mid-1920s.

clue.text: Expect bursting shells here in the island by the hill

parts.note: taken as written
Cuba is a Caribbean island
a tor is a rocky hill, as on Dartmoor

explanation.surface: A war report: expect shells to burst on an island near a hill.
explanation.walkthrough: The shells sound like artillery, but they are eggshells cracking open as chicks hatch.
explanation.definitionFit: Eggs are kept warm in a hatching machine until the chicks break out of their shells.

clue.text: Going Tory? So says the musical prince

definitions.text: Going Tory? So says the musical prince

parts.words: Going Tory? So says the musical prince
parts.note: someone moving to the Right might say '...', which names the prince of Borodin's opera

explanation.walkthrough: R stands for right, the Tory side; Prince Igor is Borodin's opera.
explanation.definitionFit: Borodin's opera Prince Igor has this hero, a medieval Russian prince.

clue.text: His man forestalled Crusoe's

parts.note: this author wrote The Man Who Was Thursday, and Thursday comes just before Robinson Crusoe's Man Friday

explanation.definitionFit: G.K. wrote The Man Who Was Thursday, and Thursday precedes Friday, Crusoe's servant.

clue.text: Tea-party dance

definitions.meaning: the 1773 protest in which colonists dumped tea in a harbour
a nineteenth-century variety of slow waltz

explanation.surface: A dance held at a tea party.
explanation.definitionFit: The Massachusetts city gave its name to the famous 1773 tea protest and to a slow waltz.

clue.text: Desire's twin guides

parts.note: A Streetcar Named Desire: a streetcar runs on a pair of rails that guide it

explanation.walkthrough: The streetcar named Desire in Tennessee Williams's play is a tram, which runs on twin rails.
explanation.definitionFit: The parallel rails that guide a streetcar along the road.

clue.text: Wiltshireman going for the moon?

parts.note: the ... were Wiltshire men who claimed to be raking the moon's reflection out of a pond, while hiding smuggled brandy

explanation.walkthrough: People from Wiltshire, an English county, are nicknamed Moonrakers after this folk tale.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who rakes, as a Wiltshire Moonraker raked for the moon in a pond.

clue.text: Point to Stevenson's prince, curious cove: speak low

definitions.note: the definition is a verb phrase while the answer is an adverbial phrase meaning in an undertone

parts.note: S, south, is a point of the compass
Robert Louis Stevenson wrote the novel Prince Otto

indicators.note: curious means odd or strange, so the letters of cove are put into an odd order

explanation.surface: Instructions to point out a prince from a Stevenson novel to some peculiar fellow, quietly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'curious' rearranges COVE into VOCE. 'Cove' is old British slang for a chap.
explanation.definitionFit: Italian for 'under the voice', the phrase describes talking in a hushed undertone.

clue.text: Go at a punishing pace

parts.note: read one way, to move along briskly at a lively speed; read another, the word for smacking someone as punishment

explanation.definitionFit: To bowl along at a smart lick is an old sense of the verb, and it also means to slap a bottom.

clue.text: For uncle a perhaps would-be bootless exercise

definitions.note: the definition is a noun phrase for the action, while the answer is the verb itself

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the letters might be arranged another way, signalling a rearrangement

explanation.surface: A futile exercise involving an uncle, of the kind that gets nowhere.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' rearranges UNCLE A. 'Bootless' looks like it means futile, but it means getting your boots off.
explanation.definitionFit: Loosening the laces is what you do before pulling off footwear, leaving you unshod.

clue.text: Unhurried thespian?

parts.note: one who saunters along at leisure, and also a travelling player of old touring companies

explanation.definitionFit: Someone who saunters is leisurely, and strolling players were itinerant actors.

clue.text: Those wearing pleats are squeezed for air

definitions.text: Those wearing pleats are squeezed for air

parts.words: Those wearing pleats are squeezed for air
parts.note: instruments with folding bellows are pressed together to push out air and play a tune

explanation.definitionFit: Squeezeboxes have pleated bellows that are compressed to play a melody, and pleated skirts are named after them.

clue.text: Diana's musical show seems to cause embarrassment

parts.note: Di is the short form of Diana, with the possessive s
a concert is a musical performance

explanation.surface: Diana's music performance seems to be an embarrassment.
explanation.definitionFit: To fluster or unsettle someone is to make them feel awkward and uneasy.

clue.text: Dorset dunes

definitions.meaning: a wealthy spit of land near Poole in Dorset, a county of southern England
ridges of sand piled up by sea or wind

explanation.surface: Sand hills on the Dorset coast.
explanation.definitionFit: A Dorset peninsula by Poole Harbour bears the name, which also means sand ridges in water.

clue.text: This ledge from nudists' tree?

parts.note: the naked Adam and Eve ate from the tree of a word that is this answer followed by ledge

explanation.walkthrough: Join the answer to LEDGE and you get the tree in Eden from which the unclothed Adam and Eve ate.
explanation.definitionFit: The answer plus 'ledge' names the forbidden tree of Genesis, so this is the first part of that word.

clue.text: In other words, laughable notions in chickens

definitions.text: In other words, laughable notions in chickens

parts.words: In other words, laughable notions in chickens
parts.note: funny bones and fancies reworded: desires plus bones, the forked bone of a fowl

explanation.definitionFit: The forked bone from a fowl's breast, pulled by two people for luck.

clue.text: Elizabeth is among Lincoln's superior ladies

indicators.note: one thing among others is placed in their midst

parts.note: Abe, Abraham Lincoln, with the possessive s
Bess is a pet form of Elizabeth

explanation.surface: Elizabeth is one of Lincoln's grand ladies.
explanation.definitionFit: Heads of convents are mothers superior.

clue.text: Scots luminary or mousy creditors

definitions.meaning: John ... Scotus was a great Scottish medieval philosopher
dun is a mousy greyish-brown colour

explanation.surface: A Scottish great man, or some timid moneylenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Duns Scotus was a famous Scottish scholastic, and debt collectors who badger people were called duns.

clue.text: They're bonneted and decked for fare

definitions.text: They're bonneted and decked for fare

parts.words: They're bonneted and decked for fare
parts.note: seems to describe people dressed up in hats and finery, but means vehicles with engine bonnets and upper decks carrying paying passengers

explanation.definitionFit: Old public road vehicles had engine covers in front and two decks, and passengers paid a fare to ride.

clue.text: She is in the little valley

parts.note: a dene is a small wooded valley
taken as written

explanation.surface: She is in a small valley.
explanation.definitionFit: A woman's first name, so a fair stand-in for a female pronoun.

clue.text: Lieutenant looks after, but is opposed

parts.note: a sub, short for subaltern, is a junior officer such as a lieutenant
tends means takes care of

explanation.surface: A lieutenant takes care of someone but is against them.
explanation.definitionFit: In geometry a side or chord is said to stretch opposite an angle, lying across from it.

clue.text: Horse South prepared to drive with the club

parts.words: prepared to drive with the club
parts.note: a golfer teed up the ball ready to drive

explanation.surface: A horse in the south was readied for a ride to the club.
explanation.definitionFit: A literary word for a mount.

clue.text: No mac, Burns? Just a boater

parts.note: without a mackintosh you get soaked
Robert Burns, so Bob for short

explanation.surface: Without a raincoat, Burns has only a straw hat to keep off the rain.
explanation.walkthrough: At Eton College a wet-bob is a boy who rows rather than plays cricket; the boater looks like the straw hat.
explanation.definitionFit: Eton slang for a pupil who takes up rowing, a person who goes out in boats.

clue.text: Goodfellow, not Robin, just a varsity red

definitions.text: Goodfellow, not Robin, just a varsity red

parts.words: Goodfellow, not Robin, just a varsity red
parts.note: not the sprite Robin Goodfellow but simply a good fellow, an old student term of praise, and a shade of red

explanation.definitionFit: A reliable, generous person was praised as one in old varsity slang, and the colour is a dull red.

clue.text: First man in Russia to organize the arts

indicators.note: the letters are organized, set into a new arrangement

explanation.surface: The first man in Russia gets the arts organized.
explanation.definitionFit: The emperor was the supreme ruler of Russia.

clue.text: Finding things weary, stale, flat and unprofitable

definitions.text: Finding things weary, stale, flat and unprofitable

parts.words: Finding things weary, stale, flat and unprofitable
parts.note: Hamlet's words for how the world seems to him in his weariness of life

explanation.definitionFit: Hamlet's soliloquy describes listless boredom with the whole world, a state of world-weariness.

clue.text: Alumnus assembly with a bee in its bonnet?

parts.note: an old boy, OB, is a former pupil
a session is a sitting or meeting

explanation.surface: A gathering of former pupils that has some fixed idea.
explanation.definitionFit: Having a bee in one's bonnet is the idiom for a fixation that keeps buzzing in the mind.

clue.text: I would turn to Edmund with a prescription

indicators.note: to turn something is to face it the other way, so these letters run backwards

parts.note: I'd is the contraction of I would
Edmund Spenser wrote The Faerie Queene

explanation.surface: Someone would go to the poet Edmund with a doctor's note.
explanation.definitionFit: A pharmacist makes up medicines given on a doctor's written order.

clue.text: Broken skies Nancy's ruin

indicators.note: broken means smashed apart, so the word skies is put back together in a new order

explanation.surface: Stormy weather brings disaster on a woman called Nancy.
explanation.walkthrough: In Dickens's Oliver Twist, Bill Sikes murders Nancy.
explanation.definitionFit: Bill Sikes, the burglar in Oliver Twist, kills Nancy, his lover.
